arXiv:2608.28007v1 [cs.LG] 28 Aug 2026

Exact Risk Ratios for Weighted Data Selection in Linear Regression

Guangjian Zhang Email: zgj1226029469@outlook.com Affiliation: University of New South Wales
Abstract

Hanneke, Moran, Shlimovich and Yehudayoff (COLT 2025) posed the following open problem. A selector sees a finite dataset D⊆ℝd×ℝD\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}, picks at most nn examples together with nonnegative weights, and hands the weighted least squares objective to the minimum-norm ERM. Writing Fw​(d,n)F_{\mathrm{w}}(d,n) for the worst-case ratio between the loss of the returned predictor on all of DD and the optimal loss, they proved Fw​(d,n)=∞F_{\mathrm{w}}(d,n)=\infty for n<dn<d, Fw​(d,d)=d+1F_{\mathrm{w}}(d,d)=d+1 and Fw​(d,n)=1F_{\mathrm{w}}(d,n)=1 for n≥2​dn\geq 2d, and asked for the value in the open regime d<n<2​dd<n<2d. We determine this value in several cases. For every dd we prove Fw​(d,2​d−1)=1+1/dF_{\mathrm{w}}(d,2d-1)=1+1/d, which confirms a claim stated without proof in the original note. We further prove Fw​(3,4)=5/3F_{\mathrm{w}}(3,4)=5/3 and Fw​(4,5)=2F_{\mathrm{w}}(4,5)=2, the two smallest cells not covered by the endpoint formula. For every intermediate budget n=d+kn=d+k we prove the lower bound Fw​(d,d+k)≥1+Γd,kF_{\mathrm{w}}(d,d+k)\geq 1+\Gamma_{d,k}, where Γd,k\Gamma_{d,k} is an explicit harmonic quantity over balanced partitions, and we show that this bound is the exact minimax value over the class of datasets whose whitened gradient systems carry an orthogonal circuit-block structure. All three exact values match 1+Γd,k1+\Gamma_{d,k}, and we conjecture that equality holds throughout the open regime. The upper bound proofs run on a common geometric spine: a rigidity theorem for positive spanning configurations of loss gradients, classifications and structural reductions of small positive bases in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} and ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4}, and a dimension-free extremal-basis argument that converts sign-cone geometry into five-point selections. We also give explicit counterexamples showing that several shorter routes fail, and constructive polynomial-time selection algorithms for all proved cases.

keywords
data selection, linear regression, empirical risk minimization, coresets, positive bases, volume sampling

1 Introduction

How well can a fixed learning rule perform on a full dataset when it is trained on only a few examples chosen from it? Hanneke et al. (2025a) initiated a systematic study of this data-selection question for empirical risk minimizers, and Hanneke et al. (2025b) distilled the open cases into a set of concrete problems. This paper addresses their Question 2, weighted data selection for linear regression.

The setting is simple to state. A dataset DD is a finite multiset in ℝd×ℝ\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R} with squared losses ℓ(x,y)​(w)=(⟨w,x⟩−y)2\ell_{(x,y)}(w)=(\langle w,x\rangle-y)^{2}. A selector, who sees all of DD, picks at most nn examples and a convex combination FF of their losses, and hands FF to the min-norm ERM A⋆A^{\star}, which returns the minimizer of FF of smallest Euclidean norm. The quantity of interest is the worst-case ratio Fw​(d,n)F_{\mathrm{w}}(d,n) between the full-data loss of the returned predictor and the optimal full-data loss; Section 2 has the formal definitions. Hanneke et al. (2025a) proved a sharp trichotomy: Fw​(d,n)F_{\mathrm{w}}(d,n) equals ∞\infty below budget dd, equals d+1d+1 at budget dd, and equals 11 from budget 2​d2d onward, where selection loses nothing at all. The two endpoint arguments have different geometries, volume sampling at n=dn=d and Steinitz’s interior-point theorem at n=2​dn=2d, and the whole regime d<n<2​dd<n<2d between them was left open, with the value known only to lie in (1,d+1](1,d+1] and to be O⁡(d)O(d).

1.1 Results

We determine the value at the top of the open regime for every dimension, and at the two smallest cells not covered by that formula.

  • •

    Budget 2​d−12d-1 (Section 3): Fw​(d,2​d−1)=1+1dF_{\mathrm{w}}(d,2d-1)=1+\frac{1}{d} for all d≥1d\geq 1. This includes Fw​(2,3)=32F_{\mathrm{w}}(2,3)=\frac{3}{2}, the smallest open cell, and proves the value that Hanneke et al. (2025b) state they believe but do not prove.

  • •

    Cell (3,4)(3,4) (Section 6): Fw​(3,4)=53F_{\mathrm{w}}(3,4)=\frac{5}{3}. This refutes the natural interpolation guess 1+(2​d−n)2/d1+(2d-n)^{2}/d, which fits all previously known values and predicts 73\frac{7}{3} here.

  • •

    Cell (4,5)(4,5) (Section 7): Fw​(4,5)=2F_{\mathrm{w}}(4,5)=2.

  • •

    A lower bound everywhere (Section 4): for all 1≤k≤d−11\leq k\leq d-1,

    Fw​(d,d+k)≥ 1+Γd,k,Γd,k=maxk+1≤s≤d⁡s−kmin∑j=1s1/rj,F_{\mathrm{w}}(d,d+k)\;\geq\;1+\Gamma_{d,k},\qquad\Gamma_{d,k}=\max_{k+1\leq s\leq d}\ \frac{s-k}{\min\sum_{j=1}^{s}1/r_{j}},

    the inner minimum over positive integer partitions r1+⋯+rs=dr_{1}+\dots+r_{s}=d, attained balanced. All three exact values above equal 1+Γd,k1+\Gamma_{d,k}.

  • •

    An exact model class (Section 5): on datasets whose whitened gradients split into orthogonal circuit blocks, the worst-case excess at budget d+kd+k is exactly Γd,k\Gamma_{d,k}, as the value of an explicit budget-allocation program. We conjecture Fw​(d,d+k)=1+Γd,kF_{\mathrm{w}}(d,d+k)=1+\Gamma_{d,k} throughout the open regime (Section 10).

Along the way we prove several structural results that may have independent interest: a rigidity theorem for gradient configurations one point below the Steinitz budget (Lemma 6), a classification of five-vector positive bases of ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} (Theorem 20), structural reductions of the minimal positive bases of ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4} of sizes 66 and 77 sufficient for the risk bounds (Propositions 37 and 41), and a dimension-free extremal-basis principle converting sign-cone geometry into selections (Lemma 45). Explicit counterexamples (Section 8) show that three shorter routes fail, which we hope clarifies where the difficulty of the general case actually lives. All upper bounds come with polynomial-time selection algorithms (Section 9).

1.2 Techniques

The endpoint theorem illustrates the method. After whitening, the full-data optimum sits at q=0q=0, the risk ratio is 1+∥q∥21+\lVert q\rVert^{2}, and the loss gradients at the optimum sum to zero. If some 2​d−12d-1 gradients positively span ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, a strictly positive zero-sum weighting turns them into a strictly convex objective whose exact minimizer is q=0q=0: selection is free. The whole difficulty is the opposite case, and the rigidity lemma shows it is extremely brittle: if no 2​d−12d-1 gradients positively span, all gradients lie on dd lines, the covariance identity forces the lines orthogonal with unit energy each, and the problem collapses to dd one-dimensional regressions, where leaving out one point on the lightest line costs exactly the harmonic factor 1d\frac{1}{d}. The matching lower bound is a translated cross-polytope whose shift punishes the min-norm tie rule for dropping any coordinate.

The two middle cells need more structure because the failure of positive spanning no longer forces an axis configuration. The classification of small positive bases replaces it: minimal positively spanning sets of gradients decompose into few circuits, extra gradients are controlled by low-rank circuits through minimal cone representations, and each resulting geometry either yields an exact certificate, or splits into orthogonal blocks, or is finished by a completion argument through quotient volume sampling. The last and hardest configuration in ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4}, two coupled triangles with two independent cross ears, which we call the rectangle, resists all partition arguments; there the extremal-basis lemma calibrates an interpolation basis on the four side rays and converts the maximal calibrated evaluation into a five-point selection through sign-cone geometry. The counterexamples of Section 8 show that this detour is not an artifact of our proof: plane-energy bounds, anchor disjunctions, and fixed-anchor generation all fail on explicit rectangle instances.

1.3 Related work

The problem sits in the data-selection program of Hanneke et al. (2025a), and is the weighted relaxation studied there and in the coreset literature; see the discussions and references in Hanneke et al. (2025b); Hanneke et al. (2025a). The budget-dd endpoint rests on volume sampling (Dereziński and Warmuth, 2017), and the budget-2​d2d endpoint on Steinitz’s theorem (Steinitz, 1916); our intermediate results can be read as interpolating between these two geometries, which the original authors anticipated would require new ideas. The theory of positive spanning sets and positive bases goes back to Davis (1954); McKinney (1962); see Regis (2016) for a modern survey, Audet (2011) for a short proof of the maximal-size theorem, and Schoch (2020) for general decomposition theorems. Our low-dimensional structure results are tailored to the risk bounds and complement this material. A recent unrefereed preprint on data selection has also appeared (Dewasurendra, 2026).

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Setting and conventions

A dataset D={zi=(xi,yi)}i=1ND=\{z_{i}=(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} is a finite multiset in ℝd×ℝ\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}. For a linear predictor w∈ℝdw\in\mathbb{R}^{d} define

ℓz​(w)=(⟨w,x⟩−y)2,LD​(w)=1N​∑i=1Nℓzi​(w),LD⋆=minw⁡LD​(w).\ell_{z}(w)=(\langle w,x\rangle-y)^{2},\qquad L_{D}(w)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\ell_{z_{i}}(w),\qquad L_{D}^{\star}=\min_{w}L_{D}(w).

The learner A⋆A^{\star} is the min-norm ERM. Given a nonnegatively weighted objective FF, the set arg⁡min⁡F\arg\min F is a translate of a linear subspace, and A⋆​(F)A^{\star}(F) is its unique element of smallest Euclidean norm. Weighted selection with budget nn means choosing z1,…,zn∈Dz_{1},\dots,z_{n}\in D and F∈conv⁡(ℓz1,…,ℓzn)F\in\mathrm{conv}(\ell_{z_{1}},\dots,\ell_{z_{n}}). Define

LD⋆​(n,A⋆)=infz1,…,zn,FLD​(A⋆​(F)),Fw​(d,n)=supDLD⋆​(n,A⋆)LD⋆,L_{D}^{\star}(n;A^{\star})=\inf_{z_{1},\dots,z_{n},\;F}L_{D}\bigl(A^{\star}(F)\bigr),\qquad F_{\mathrm{w}}(d,n)=\sup_{D}\frac{L_{D}^{\star}(n;A^{\star})}{L_{D}^{\star}},

with the conventions 0/0=10/0=1 and c/0=∞c/0=\infty for c>0c>0; these conventions appear in Theorem 8 of Hanneke et al. (2025a). Repetitions are allowed and zero weights are permitted, so we count selections by effective support: a repeated point merges its weights, a zero-weight point counts as unselected, and an objective supported on fewer than nn points fills its remaining slots with repetitions. Throughout, “a selection of at most nn points” refers to effective support size.

Hanneke et al. (2025b); Hanneke et al. (2025a) determined three regimes. Fw​(d,n)=∞F_{\mathrm{w}}(d,n)=\infty for n<dn<d, and the lower bound holds for every weakly continuous ERM. Fw​(d,d)=d+1F_{\mathrm{w}}(d,d)=d+1, with the upper bound via size-dd volume sampling (Dereziński and Warmuth, 2017). Fw​(d,n)=1F_{\mathrm{w}}(d,n)=1 for n≥2​dn\geq 2d, via Steinitz’s interior version of Carathéodory’s theorem (Steinitz, 1916). For d<n<2​dd<n<2d the value is known to lie in (1,d+1](1,d+1] and to be O⁡(d)O(d) (Hanneke et al., 2025a, Section 4), and the regime is posed as Question 2 of Hanneke et al. (2025b). The note adds: “In the case n=2​d−1n=2d-1, we believe we have an argument showing that the value is exactly 1+1d1+\frac{1}{d}, though the argument is somewhat ad hoc and does not clearly extend to other values of nn” (Hanneke et al., 2025b, p. 3).

We use the following form of Steinitz’s theorem (Steinitz, 1916). If a point lies in the interior of the convex hull of a finite set S⊆ℝmS\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m}, then it lies in the interior of the convex hull of some subset of SS of size at most 2​m2m. The interior is taken in ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m}; when we apply the theorem inside a subspace VV, we first check that the affine hull of SS is all of VV, so that relative interior means interior in the ambient space VV, and the conclusion returns a subset whose convex hull still has the point as a VV-interior point. In particular the affine hull of the returned subset is again VV.

2.2 Whitening

Lemma 1 (whitening).

Let H=1N​∑ixi​xi⊤≻0H=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\succ 0 and LD⋆>0L_{D}^{\star}>0. Let w⋆w^{\star} be the unique full-data optimum and ri=yi−⟨w⋆,xi⟩r_{i}=y_{i}-\langle w^{\star},x_{i}\rangle. Set

ξi=H−1/2xi,ηi=riLD⋆,q=H1/2​(w−w⋆)LD⋆.\xi_{i}=H^{-1/2}x_{i},\qquad\eta_{i}=\frac{r_{i}}{\sqrt{L_{D}^{\star}}},\qquad q=\frac{H^{1/2}(w-w^{\star})}{\sqrt{L_{D}^{\star}}}.

Then

1N​∑iξi​ξi⊤=Id,1N​∑iηi​ξi=0,1N​∑iηi2=1,\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\xi_{i}\xi_{i}^{\top}=I_{d},\qquad\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\eta_{i}\xi_{i}=0,\qquad\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\eta_{i}^{2}=1, (1)

and for every ww,

LD​(w)LD⋆=1+∥q∥2.\frac{L_{D}(w)}{L_{D}^{\star}}=1+\lVert q\rVert^{2}. (2)
Proof.

The first identity is H−1/2HH−1/2=IdH^{-1/2}HH^{-1/2}=I_{d}. The second is the normal equation 1N​∑iri​xi=0\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}r_{i}x_{i}=0. The third is the definition of LD⋆L_{D}^{\star}. For (2), note ⟨w,xi⟩−yi=LD⋆​(⟨q,ξi⟩−ηi)\langle w,x_{i}\rangle-y_{i}=\sqrt{L_{D}^{\star}}\,(\langle q,\xi_{i}\rangle-\eta_{i}) and expand the square; the cross term vanishes by the second identity. ∎

We call a finite family {(ξi,ηi)}i=1N⊆ℝd×ℝ\{(\xi_{i},\eta_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R} satisfying (1) a whitened system. Write gi=ηi​ξig_{i}=\eta_{i}\xi_{i}; up to a common positive factor this is the gradient of ℓi\ell_{i} at q=0q=0, and ∑igi=0\sum_{i}g_{i}=0. Whitening is not an orthogonal map, so it does not commute with the min-norm tie rule. We therefore use whitened coordinates only to compute the risk ratio (2) and to build selections whose objectives are strictly convex; such objectives have a unique minimizer and the tie rule never acts. All branches that could produce rank-deficient objectives are handled separately, either in the original coordinates or through finite penalty approximations.

A whitened system is itself a legal dataset: take xi=ξix_{i}=\xi_{i}, yi=ηiy_{i}=\eta_{i}. Then H=IdH=I_{d}, w⋆=0w^{\star}=0 and LD⋆=1L_{D}^{\star}=1, and the Euclidean min-norm rule in the original coordinates of this dataset is the min-norm rule in whitened coordinates. We call this the self-realization of the system, and use it to transfer dataset-level statements to whitened systems without any change of coordinates.

Lemma 2 (exact certificate).

Let SS be a set of indices with weights αi>0\alpha_{i}>0 such that ∑i∈Sαi​gi=0\sum_{i\in S}\alpha_{i}g_{i}=0 and span⁡{ξi:i∈S}=ℝd\operatorname{span}\{\xi_{i}:i\in S\}=\mathbb{R}^{d}. Then q=0q=0 is the unique minimizer of ∑i∈Sαi​(⟨q,ξi⟩−ηi)2\sum_{i\in S}\alpha_{i}(\langle q,\xi_{i}\rangle-\eta_{i})^{2}, and the corresponding selection has risk ratio 11.

Proof.

The gradient of the objective at q=0q=0 is −2∑i∈Sαigi=0-2\sum_{i\in S}\alpha_{i}g_{i}=0. The Hessian is 2​∑i∈Sαi​ξi​ξi⊤2\sum_{i\in S}\alpha_{i}\xi_{i}\xi_{i}^{\top}, positive definite because the weights are positive and the features span. Zero-gradient points may be added to SS with any positive weights: their gi=0g_{i}=0 keeps the stationarity, and extra features only help the Hessian. ∎

Lemma 3 (volume sampling interface).

Let {(ζi,ηi)}i=1M⊆ℝr×ℝ\{(\zeta_{i},\eta_{i})\}_{i=1}^{M}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{r}\times\mathbb{R} have features spanning ℝr\mathbb{R}^{r}, and let ρ⁡(u)=1M​∑i(⟨u,ζi⟩−ηi)2\rho(u)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i}(\langle u,\zeta_{i}\rangle-\eta_{i})^{2} with minimum ρ⋆\rho^{\star}. Then there are rr indices with linearly independent features whose interpolation point u^\hat{u} (the unique solution of ⟨u^,ζi⟩=ηi\langle\hat{u},\zeta_{i}\rangle=\eta_{i} on those indices) satisfies ρ⁡(u^)≤(r+1)​ρ⋆\rho(\hat{u})\leq(r+1)\rho^{\star}.

Proof.

The family is a legal dataset with features ζi\zeta_{i} and labels ηi\eta_{i}. By Theorem 5 of Dereziński and Warmuth (2017), under size-rr volume sampling, which assigns to a subset SS probability proportional to det(ZS​ZS⊤)\det(Z_{S}Z_{S}^{\top}), the expected full-data loss of the least squares solution on SS is at most (r+1)​ρ⋆(r+1)\rho^{\star}, with equality in general position. The distribution charges only subsets with independent features, and on such subsets the least squares solution is the interpolation point, independent of any weights. Some subset attains the expectation or better. If ρ⋆=0\rho^{\star}=0, any independent subset interpolates the realizable labels exactly. ∎

Note that in Lemma 3 the interpolation point does not depend on weights, so the min-norm rule is irrelevant on these full-rank supports.

2.3 Positive spanning sets

A finite set B⊆ℝm∖{0}B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m}\setminus\{0\} positively spans ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m} if pos⁡(B)=ℝm\operatorname{pos}(B)=\mathbb{R}^{m}, where pos\operatorname{pos} denotes the set of nonnegative combinations. BB is a positive basis if in addition no proper subset positively spans. A positive circuit is a finite set carrying a linear dependence with all coefficients strictly positive, minimal with respect to support; a positive circuit of size m+1m+1 has rank mm. The next lemma is classical: the size bounds and the antipodal structure of maximal positive bases are due to Davis (1954) and McKinney (1962); see Audet (2011) for a short proof and Regis (2016); Schoch (2020) for general structure theory.

Lemma 4.

Every positive basis BB of ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m} satisfies m+1≤|B|≤2​mm+1\leq|B|\leq 2m. If |B|=2​m|B|=2m then there is a linear basis a1,…,ama_{1},\dots,a_{m} and positive scalars λj\lambda_{j} with B={a1,−λ1​a1,…,am,−λm​am}B=\{a_{1},-\lambda_{1}a_{1},\dots,a_{m},-\lambda_{m}a_{m}\}.

Lemma 5.

Let V={v1,…,vp}V=\{v_{1},\dots,v_{p}\} positively span ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m}.

  1. 1.

    There are coefficients λi>0\lambda_{i}>0 with ∑iλi​vi=0\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}v_{i}=0.

  2. 2.

    If p=m+1p=m+1 then VV spans linearly, its kernel is one-dimensional, and the kernel is generated by a strictly positive vector; so VV is a positive circuit of rank mm.

  3. 3.

    Let K⊆ℝpK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{p} be a linear subspace and let λ\lambda generate an extreme ray of K∩ℝ+pK\cap\mathbb{R}^{p}_{+}. Then the columns indexed by S=supp⁡(λ)S=\operatorname{supp}(\lambda) carry a one-dimensional dependence space; if KK is the kernel of a matrix with columns viv_{i}, the support SS is a positive circuit.

Proof.

(1) For each ii write −vi=∑jβi​j​vj-v_{i}=\sum_{j}\beta_{ij}v_{j} with βi​j≥0\beta_{ij}\geq 0 and sum over ii; the combined identity ∑j(1+∑iβi​j)​vj=0\sum_{j}(1+\sum_{i}\beta_{ij})v_{j}=0 has all coefficients at least 11. (2) The positive cone is contained in the linear span, so VV spans and the kernel has dimension one; part (1) puts a strictly positive vector in it, so the unique dependence is strictly positive and supported everywhere. (3) If the dependence space on SS had dimension two, take μ\mu in KK supported in SS and not proportional to λ\lambda. Since λ\lambda is strictly positive on SS, both λ±ε​μ\lambda\pm\varepsilon\mu lie in the cone for small ε>0\varepsilon>0, and λ\lambda is their midpoint, contradicting extremality. ∎

We use one nonclassical rigidity statement. Its content is that failing to positively span with one point below the Steinitz budget forces an axis structure.

Lemma 6 (rigidity).

Let G⊆ℝm∖{0}G\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m}\setminus\{0\} positively span ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m}, and suppose no subset of GG of size at most 2​m−12m-1 positively spans ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m}. Then there is a linear basis a1,…,ama_{1},\dots,a_{m} such that every element of GG lies on one of the lines ℝ​aj\mathbb{R}a_{j}.

All elements of TT lie in GG up to positive scaling, so this contradicts the hypothesis. Hence |S|=1|S|=1. ∎

Finally we record a quotient lemma used when passing from a positive basis to a smaller one.

Lemma 7 (quotient minimality).

Let BB be a minimum-cardinality positively spanning subset of a set of vectors in ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m}, let C⊆BC\subseteq B be a positive circuit with V=span⁡(C)=pos⁡(C)V=\operatorname{span}(C)=\operatorname{pos}(C), and let π:ℝm→ℝm/V\pi:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}/V be the quotient map. Then π⁡(b)≠0\pi(b)\neq 0 for every b∈B∖Cb\in B\setminus C, and π⁡(B∖C)\pi(B\setminus C) is a positive basis of ℝm/V\mathbb{R}^{m}/V.

Proof.

π⁡(B∖C)\pi(B\setminus C) positively spans the quotient because BB positively spans ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m}. If π⁡(b)=0\pi(b)=0 then b∈V=pos⁡(C)⊆pos⁡(B∖{b})b\in V=\operatorname{pos}(C)\subseteq\operatorname{pos}(B\setminus\{b\}), since C⊆B∖{b}C\subseteq B\setminus\{b\}; hence B∖{b}B\setminus\{b\} still positively spans, contradicting minimality. If some π⁡(b)\pi(b) were removable in the quotient, then for every x∈ℝmx\in\mathbb{R}^{m} we could write π⁡(x)\pi(x) as a nonnegative combination of π⁡(B∖C∖{b})\pi(B\setminus C\setminus\{b\}), lift, and absorb the error in V=pos⁡(C)V=\operatorname{pos}(C); this exhibits x∈pos⁡(B∖{b})x\in\operatorname{pos}(B\setminus\{b\}), again contradicting minimality. ∎

3 The budget 2​d−12d-1

This section proves Fw​(d,2​d−1)=1+1/dF_{\mathrm{w}}(d,2d-1)=1+1/d for every d≥1d\geq 1. The upper bound is organized as an interface theorem about whitened systems; later sections call it in dimensions 22 and 33.

3.1 The whitened upper bound

Theorem 8 (whitened endpoint interface).

Let {(ξi,ηi)}i=1N\{(\xi_{i},\eta_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} be a whitened system in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Then there exist at most 2​d−12d-1 indices and strictly positive weights whose objective G⁡(q)=∑αi​(⟨q,ξi⟩−ηi)2G(q)=\sum\alpha_{i}(\langle q,\xi_{i}\rangle-\eta_{i})^{2} is strictly convex with unique minimizer q^\hat{q} satisfying

In particular their affine hull is again VV, so these gradients span VV, and VV-interiority provides strictly positive coefficients αi\alpha_{i} with ∑αi​gi=0\sum\alpha_{i}g_{i}=0. The features of all nonzero-gradient points lie in VV, while all features together span ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}; hence points with gi=0g_{i}=0 and ξi∉V\xi_{i}\notin V exist and their features span ℝd/V\mathbb{R}^{d}/V. By Lemma 2 the selection recovers q=0q=0 exactly with at most 2​r+(d−r)=d+r≤2​d−12r+(d-r)=d+r\leq 2d-1 points.

5 Orthogonal circuit-block systems: an exact minimax value

The instances of Section 4 live in a natural model class, and on this class the harmonic quantity Γd,k\Gamma_{d,k} is not merely a lower bound but the exact minimax answer. This is the content of the present section.

Definition 14.

A whitened system {(ξi,ηi)}\{(\xi_{i},\eta_{i})\} in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} has orthogonal circuit-block structure with dimension vector r=(r1,…,rs)r=(r_{1},\dots,r_{s}), ∑jrj=d\sum_{j}r_{j}=d, if ℝd=E1⊕⟂⋯⊕⟂Es\mathbb{R}^{d}=E_{1}\oplus^{\perp}\dots\oplus^{\perp}E_{s} with dimEj=rj\dim E_{j}=r_{j}, every nonzero feature lies in some EjE_{j}, and every EjE_{j} contains a positive circuit of rj+1r_{j}+1 gradients spanning EjE_{j}. Here a positive circuit of gradients means a set of indices whose gradients gi=ηi​ξig_{i}=\eta_{i}\xi_{i} carry a strictly positive zero-sum relation, minimal with respect to support. Write Ij={i:ξi∈Ej∖{0}}I_{j}=\{i:\xi_{i}\in E_{j}\setminus\{0\}\} and Rj=1N​∑i∈Ijηi2R_{j}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i\in I_{j}}\eta_{i}^{2}, so ∑jRj≤1\sum_{j}R_{j}\leq 1; points with ξi=0\xi_{i}=0 belong to no block. The model class 𝒟r\mathcal{D}_{r} consists of the datasets DD with full feature rank and LD⋆>0L_{D}^{\star}>0 whose whitened system under Lemma 1 has orthogonal circuit-block structure with dimension vector rr.

The class is defined at the level of datasets, not of whitened systems alone, and this matters. A whitened system does not determine the min-norm tie rule of the underlying dataset, because whitening is not orthogonal; and for the self-realized dataset of a whitened system the tie rule actively helps the selector, since there the full-data optimum is the origin and unconstrained directions are resolved to it for free. The statements below avoid this issue from both sides: the upper bound uses only strictly convex selections, which are tie-rule-free and therefore valid for every dataset in 𝒟r\mathcal{D}_{r}, and the lower bound uses the original-coordinate instances of Proposition 12, whose large parameter shift makes the tie rule costly.

Since the blocks are orthogonal and each block’s nonzero features lie inside it, the covariance identity forces 1N​∑i∈Ijξi​ξi⊤\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i\in I_{j}}\xi_{i}\xi_{i}^{\top} to equal the orthogonal projector onto EjE_{j}, and the normal equation projects to zero in each block.

Theorem 15 (exact budget–energy value).

Let D∈𝒟rD\in\mathcal{D}_{r} and let its whitened system have energies (Rj)(R_{j}); let the budget be n=d+kn=d+k with 0≤k≤s−10\leq k\leq s-1. Then there is a strictly convex, strictly positively weighted selection of at most d+kd+k points with

∥q^∥2≤min⁡∑j∉KK⊆[s],|K|=k⁡rj​Rj,\lVert\hat{q}\rVert^{2}\;\leq\;\min_{K\subseteq[s],\,|K|=k}\ \sum_{j\notin K}r_{j}R_{j},

and the supremum of the right-hand side over admissible energies is exactly

Φ⁡(r,k)=maxJ⊆[s],|J|≥k+1⁡|J|−k∑j∈J1/rj.\Phi(r,k)=\max_{J\subseteq[s],\,|J|\geq k+1}\frac{|J|-k}{\sum_{j\in J}1/r_{j}}. (9)

For k≥sk\geq s the budget completes every block and the excess is zero.

Proof.

Selection. Fix KK with |K|=k|K|=k. For j∈Kj\in K select the full circuit of block jj with its strictly positive zero-sum weights: rj+1r_{j}+1 points, and by Lemma 2 applied inside EjE_{j} the block output is 00. For j∉Kj\notin K, view the points indexed by IjI_{j} as a dataset in Ej≅ℝrjE_{j}\cong\mathbb{R}^{r_{j}}; zero-feature points belong to no block and are never selected. Its covariance is a positive multiple of the identity and its normal equation vanishes, so its optimal parameter is 00 and its optimal risk is (N/Mj)​Rj(N/M_{j})R_{j}, where Mj=|Ij|M_{j}=|I_{j}|. 6 The budget 44 in dimension 33

This section proves Fw​(3,4)=53F_{\mathrm{w}}(3,4)=\frac{5}{3}. The lower bound is Theorem 13 at (d,k)=(3,1)(d,k)=(3,1). The upper bound requires new structure: a complete classification of five-vector positive bases of ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} and a covering theorem for the gradients outside such a basis.

6.1 Penalty limits and anchors

Lemma 17 (multi-anchor penalty limit).

Let CC have full row rank, 𝒜={q:C​q=b}\mathcal{A}=\{q:Cq=b\}, and let G≥0G\geq 0 be a convex quadratic whose restriction to 𝒜\mathcal{A} has a unique minimizer q𝒜q_{\mathcal{A}}. Assume the Hessian nullspace of GG meets ker⁡C\ker C only at 00. Then for every λ>0\lambda>0 the function Fλ​(q)=G⁡(q)+λ​∥C​q−b∥2F_{\lambda}(q)=G(q)+\lambda\lVert Cq-b\rVert^{2} is strictly convex, and its unique minimizer qλq_{\lambda} converges to q𝒜q_{\mathcal{A}} as λ→∞\lambda\to\infty.

Proof.

Strict convexity is the nullspace condition. Optimality gives Fλ​(qλ)≤Fλ​(q𝒜)=G⁡(q𝒜)F_{\lambda}(q_{\lambda})\leq F_{\lambda}(q_{\mathcal{A}})=G(q_{\mathcal{A}}), so G⁡(qλ)≤G⁡(q𝒜)G(q_{\lambda})\leq G(q_{\mathcal{A}}) and λ​∥C​qλ−b∥2≤G⁡(q𝒜)\lambda\lVert Cq_{\lambda}-b\rVert^{2}\leq G(q_{\mathcal{A}}), using G≥0G\geq 0; the constraint violation tends to 00. Decompose qλ=vλ+wλq_{\lambda}=v_{\lambda}+w_{\lambda} with wλ∈ker⁡Cw_{\lambda}\in\ker C and vλ⟂ker⁡Cv_{\lambda}\perp\ker C. The component vλv_{\lambda} is bounded because C​qλCq_{\lambda} is bounded and CC is injective on (ker⁡C)⟂(\ker C)^{\perp}. On the affine sets {Cq=Cqλ}\{Cq=Cq_{\lambda}\} the quadratic GG is strictly convex in the ker⁡C\ker C direction, uniformly in the translate, so the sublevel set {G≤G(q𝒜)}\{G\leq G(q_{\mathcal{A}})\} intersected with bounded constraint violation is bounded in wλw_{\lambda} as well. Any accumulation point of qλq_{\lambda} lies in 𝒜\mathcal{A} and minimizes GG there, hence equals q𝒜q_{\mathcal{A}}. ∎

When each row of CC is a feature ξi⊤\xi_{i}^{\top} and bi=ηib_{i}=\eta_{i}, the penalty λ​∥C​q−b∥2\lambda\lVert Cq-b\rVert^{2} is a positive combination of original losses. Every finite λ\lambda therefore yields a legal, strictly positively weighted, strictly convex objective, and the risk of its output approaches the risk of q𝒜q_{\mathcal{A}}. Since LD⋆​(n,A⋆)L_{D}^{\star}(n;A^{\star}) is an infimum, limits of this kind suffice for upper bounds.

Lemma 18 (anchored reduction in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}).

Let a whitened system in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} contain a point with η0=0\eta_{0}=0 and ξ0≠0\xi_{0}\neq 0. Then for every ε>0\varepsilon>0 there is a strictly convex, strictly positively weighted selection of at most 44 points with 1+∥q^∥2≤32+ε1+\lVert\hat{q}\rVert^{2}\leq\frac{3}{2}+\varepsilon.

Proof.

Let W=ξ0⟂W=\xi_{0}^{\perp} and ζi=PW​ξi\zeta_{i}=P_{W}\xi_{i}. The projected family {(ζi,ηi)}\{(\zeta_{i},\eta_{i})\} satisfies the three identities (1) on W≅ℝ2W\cong\mathbb{R}^{2}: the covariance projects to PW​PW=IWP_{W}P_{W}=I_{W}, the normal equation and the energy are unchanged. Apply Theorem 8 with d=2d=2 to get at most 33 indices and positive weights whose objective GG, formed from the original three-dimensional losses, is strictly convex on WW with unique minimizer qW∈Wq_{W}\in W satisfying 1+∥qW∥2≤321+\lVert q_{W}\rVert^{2}\leq\frac{3}{2}. The selected features control only their WW-components; strict convexity on WW holds because the chosen ζ\zeta’s span WW. Add the anchor constraint ⟨q,ξ0⟩=0\langle q,\xi_{0}\rangle=0 through Lemma 17: the penalty is the anchor point’s own loss, the nullspace condition holds since a direction killed by both GG and the anchor would lie in WW and contradict strict convexity there, and qλ→qWq_{\lambda}\to q_{W}. A large finite λ\lambda gives a four-point selection within ε\varepsilon. ∎

Consequently, in the branches below we may assume

gi=0⟹ξi=0,g_{i}=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \xi_{i}=0, (10)

because a point with ηi=0≠ξi\eta_{i}=0\neq\xi_{i} triggers Lemma 18 and the bound 32<53\frac{3}{2}<\frac{5}{3}.

Lemma 19 (plane energy).

Let CC be a positive circuit of three gradients of rank 22 with plane P=span⁡{gi:i∈C}P=\operatorname{span}\{g_{i}:i\in C\} and weights αi>0\alpha_{i}>0, ∑i∈Cαi​gi=0\sum_{i\in C}\alpha_{i}g_{i}=0. Define R(P)=1N∑i:ξi∈Pηi2R(P)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i:\xi_{i}\in P}\eta_{i}^{2}, where points with ξi=0\xi_{i}=0 count as members of PP. Then under (10) there is a strictly convex four-point selection with ∥q^∥2≤1−R⁡(P)\lVert\hat{q}\rVert^{2}\leq 1-R(P).

Proof.

Let uu be a unit normal of PP. Every point with ξj∉P\xi_{j}\notin P has ⟨u,ξj⟩≠0\langle u,\xi_{j}\rangle\neq 0 and, by (10), ηj≠0\eta_{j}\neq 0. The covariance identity gives ∑j:ξj∉P⟨u,ξj⟩2=N\sum_{j:\xi_{j}\notin P}\langle u,\xi_{j}\rangle^{2}=N, so by weighted averaging some jj has ηj2/⟨u,ξj⟩2≤1N​∑ξj∉Pηj2=1−R⁡(P)\eta_{j}^{2}/\langle u,\xi_{j}\rangle^{2}\leq\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\xi_{j}\notin P}\eta_{j}^{2}=1-R(P). Select the circuit with its weights and the point jj, and let qj=(ηj/⟨u,ξj⟩)​uq_{j}=\bigl(\eta_{j}/\langle u,\xi_{j}\rangle\bigr)u. Circuit residuals at qjq_{j} are −ηi-\eta_{i} since qj⟂Pq_{j}\perp P, so the circuit part of the gradient is −2∑αigi=0-2\sum\alpha_{i}g_{i}=0; point jj is interpolated at qjq_{j}. The features span ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}, so qjq_{j} is the unique minimizer, and ∥qj∥2≤1−R⁡(P)\lVert q_{j}\rVert^{2}\leq 1-R(P). ∎

6.2 Five-vector positive bases of ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}

Theorem 20 (classification).

Let B={b1,…,b5}B=\{b_{1},\dots,b_{5}\} be a positive basis of ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}. Up to renumbering, independent positive rescaling of each vector, and an invertible linear map,

b1=e1,b2=e2,b3=−e1−e2,b4=e3−κ2​e1,b5=−e3−κ2​e1,b_{1}=e_{1},\quad b_{2}=e_{2},\quad b_{3}=-e_{1}-e_{2},\quad b_{4}=e_{3}-\tfrac{\kappa}{2}e_{1},\quad b_{5}=-e_{3}-\tfrac{\kappa}{2}e_{1},

for some κ≥0\kappa\geq 0; equivalently

b1+b2+b3=0,κ​b1+b4+b5=0.b_{1}+b_{2}+b_{3}=0,\qquad\kappa b_{1}+b_{4}+b_{5}=0. (11)

For κ=0\kappa=0 the basis splits into a rank-22 triangle circuit and an antipodal pair; all κ>0\kappa>0 form one orbit, in which two rank-22 triangle circuits share the vector b1b_{1}.

Proof.

Let KK be the kernel of the 3×53\times 5 matrix with columns bib_{i}; dimK=2\dim K=2. The cone 𝒞=K∩ℝ+5\mathcal{C}=K\cap\mathbb{R}^{5}_{+} contains a strictly positive vector by Lemma 5(1), so it is a two-dimensional pointed cone with exactly two extreme rays. By Lemma 5(3) each extreme ray is supported on a positive circuit. A circuit of rank 33 would positively span ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} with at most four elements, contradicting minimality of BB; so both circuits have rank at most 22 and support size at most 33. The strictly positive vector is a positive combination of the two rays, so the two supports cover {1,…,5}\{1,\dots,5\}. Two supports of size at most 33 covering five coordinates are either disjoint of sizes 3,23,2, or of sizes 3,33,3 sharing one coordinate. The first case is a triangle circuit plus an antipodal pair; the second is two triangles sharing one vector, whose planes differ since the matrix has rank 33. Normalizing the first triangle to e1,e2,−e1−e2e_{1},e_{2},-e_{1}-e_{2} and the second relation to κ​b1+b4+b5=0\kappa b_{1}+b_{4}+b_{5}=0, and sending (b4−b5)/2(b_{4}-b_{5})/2 to e3e_{3}, yields the stated form. A diagonal map diag⁡(λ,λ,μ)\mathrm{diag}(\lambda,\lambda,\mu) rescales κ\kappa by λ/μ\lambda/\mu, so all κ>0\kappa>0 are equivalent. ∎

6.3 The coupled branch: a three-plane cover

Fix a coupled basis, positively normalized as

a1+a2+a3=0,κ​a1+a4+a5=0,κ>0,a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}=0,\qquad\kappa a_{1}+a_{4}+a_{5}=0,\qquad\kappa>0, (12)

and write PA=span⁡(a1,a2)P_{A}=\operatorname{span}(a_{1},a_{2}), PB=span⁡(a1,a4)P_{B}=\operatorname{span}(a_{1},a_{4}).

Lemma 21.

Assume no four gradients form a positive circuit of rank 33. Then every nonzero gradient gg outside the basis satisfies −g=α​ai-g=\alpha a_{i} or −g=α​ai+β​aj-g=\alpha a_{i}+\beta a_{j} with α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0.

Proof.

−g∈pos⁡(B)-g\in\operatorname{pos}(B); take a support-minimal nonnegative representation. Its support is linearly independent, else a dependence could shrink it. A support of size 33 would give, together with gg, a four-point positive circuit of rank 33. ∎

Call gg of type i​jij in the second case. Types inside one triangle lie in its plane: types 12,13,2312,13,23 lie in PAP_{A} and types 14,15,4514,15,45 in PBP_{B}. The remaining types 24,25,34,3524,25,34,35 are called cross types.

Lemma 22.

Assume no four gradients form a positive circuit of rank 33. Then at most one cross type occurs.

Proof.

Let p=−α​au−β​avp=-\alpha a_{u}-\beta a_{v} and q=−γ​au′−δ​av′q=-\gamma a_{u^{\prime}}-\delta a_{v^{\prime}} with u,u′∈{2,3}u,u^{\prime}\in\{2,3\}, v,v′∈{4,5}v,v^{\prime}\in\{4,5\}, (u,v)≠(u′,v′)(u,v)\neq(u^{\prime},v^{\prime}). In each of the three cases we exhibit a four-point positive circuit, contradiction. If u=u′u=u^{\prime}, v≠v′v\neq v^{\prime}, compute using (12), for u=2u=2: δ​p+β​q=−(δ​α+β​γ+β​δ​κ)​a2−β​δ​κ​a3\delta p+\beta q=-(\delta\alpha+\beta\gamma+\beta\delta\kappa)a_{2}-\beta\delta\kappa a_{3}, so {p,q,a2,a3}\{p,q,a_{2},a_{3}\} carries a positive dependence, and its rank is 33 since p,qp,q leave the plane PAP_{A}. If v=v′v=v^{\prime}, u≠u′u\neq u^{\prime}, for v=4v=4: γ​p+α​q=−(α​γκ+γ​β+α​δ)​a4−α​γκ​a5\gamma p+\alpha q=-\bigl(\tfrac{\alpha\gamma}{\kappa}+\gamma\beta+\alpha\delta\bigr)a_{4}-\tfrac{\alpha\gamma}{\kappa}a_{5}, same conclusion with a4,a5a_{4},a_{5}. If u≠u′u\neq u^{\prime} and v≠v′v\neq v^{\prime}: δ​p+β​q=−(δ​α+β​δ​κ)​au−(β​γ+β​δ​κ)​au′\delta p+\beta q=-(\delta\alpha+\beta\delta\kappa)a_{u}-(\beta\gamma+\beta\delta\kappa)a_{u^{\prime}}, same conclusion with au,au′a_{u},a_{u^{\prime}}. ∎

Lemma 23 (three-plane cover).

Assume no four gradients form a positive circuit of rank 33. Then all nonzero gradients lie in PA∪PBP_{A}\cup P_{B}, or in PA∪PB∪Pu​vP_{A}\cup P_{B}\cup P_{uv} for a single cross type (u,v)(u,v) with Pu​v=span⁡(au,av)P_{uv}=\operatorname{span}(a_{u},a_{v}). Each listed plane contains a rank-22 positive triangle circuit.

Proof.

Lemma 21 reduces every extra gradient to a ray or a two-element cone type. The six in-triangle types lie in PA∪PBP_{A}\cup P_{B}, and by Lemma 22 at most one cross type (u,v)(u,v) occurs; its members lie in Pu​vP_{uv}. Rays lie in these planes as well. PAP_{A} and PBP_{B} contain the two basis triangles; if the cross plane occurs, au,ava_{u},a_{v} together with any cross gradient of that type form a positive triangle circuit spanning Pu​vP_{uv}. ∎

Proposition 24 (coupled branch).

Under (10), if the nonzero gradients contain a coupled five-vector positive basis and no four of them form a rank-33 positive circuit, then some four-point strictly convex selection has ∥q^∥2≤23\lVert\hat{q}\rVert^{2}\leq\frac{2}{3}.

Proof.

By Lemma 23 the nonzero features, which are collinear with their gradients, lie in at most three planes, each carrying a positive triangle circuit; points with ξi=0\xi_{i}=0 lie in every plane. The three plane energies cover total energy 11, so some plane has R⁡(P)≥13R(P)\geq\frac{1}{3}; with two planes, some plane has R⁡(P)≥12R(P)\geq\frac{1}{2}. Lemma 19 gives ∥q^∥2≤1−R⁡(P)≤23\lVert\hat{q}\rVert^{2}\leq 1-R(P)\leq\frac{2}{3}. ∎

6.4 The split branch and the six-axis branch

Proposition 25 (split branch).

Under (10), suppose the nonzero gradients contain a κ=0\kappa=0 basis, i.e. a rank-22 triangle circuit with plane VV and an antipodal pair on a line LL with V⊕L=ℝ3V\oplus L=\mathbb{R}^{3}, and suppose all nonzero gradients lie in V∪LV\cup L. Then some four-point strictly convex selection has ∥q^∥2≤23\lVert\hat{q}\rVert^{2}\leq\frac{2}{3}.

Proof.

All nonzero features lie in V∪LV\cup L by (10). Write HV,HLH_{V},H_{L} for the feature second moments of the two groups; then I=HV+HLI=H_{V}+H_{L} with rank⁡HV=2\operatorname{rank}H_{V}=2, rank⁡HL=1\operatorname{rank}H_{L}=1. Writing HL=λ​u​u⊤H_{L}=\lambda uu^{\top}, the rank of HV=I−λ​u​u⊤H_{V}=I-\lambda uu^{\top} equals 22 only if λ=1\lambda=1; hence L=ℝ​uL=\mathbb{R}u, V=u⟂V=u^{\perp}, HV=PVH_{V}=P_{V}, HL=PLH_{L}=P_{L}. Assign points with ξi=0\xi_{i}=0 to the VV group and write RV+RL≤1R_{V}+R_{L}\leq 1 for the group energies. The normal equation splits along the orthogonal decomposition, so both groups have optimum 00.

Selection A: the full triangle circuit in VV plus the best single point on LL. On LL, 1N​∑ti2=1\frac{1}{N}\sum t_{i}^{2}=1, and the weighted-average argument of Theorem 8 yields a point with squared offset at most RLR_{L}; the circuit fixes the VV component at 00. Hence ΔA≤RL\Delta_{A}\leq R_{L} with 44 points.

Selection B: an antipodal pair on LL with canceling weights, plus a volume-sampling pair in VV. The VV group, viewed as a dataset in V≅ℝ2V\cong\mathbb{R}^{2} of size NVN_{V}, has covariance (N/NV)​IV(N/N_{V})I_{V} and optimal risk (N/NV)​RV(N/N_{V})R_{V}. Lemma 3 with r=2r=2 gives two independent features whose interpolation point uVu_{V} satisfies (N/NV)​(RV+∥uV∥2)≤3​(N/NV)​RV(N/N_{V})\bigl(R_{V}+\lVert u_{V}\rVert^{2}\bigr)\leq 3(N/N_{V})R_{V}, so ∥uV∥2≤2​RV\lVert u_{V}\rVert^{2}\leq 2R_{V}. The pair fixes the LL component at 00; the joint objective is strictly convex on ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} and separates, so ΔB≤2​RV\Delta_{B}\leq 2R_{V} with 44 points.

Finally min⁡{RL,2​RV}≤23\min\{R_{L},2R_{V}\}\leq\frac{2}{3} whenever RV+RL≤1R_{V}+R_{L}\leq 1. ∎

Proposition 26 (six-axis branch).

Under (10), suppose the minimum-cardinality positively spanning subset of the nonzero gradients has size 66 and all nonzero gradients lie on its three lines. Then some four-point strictly convex selection has ∥q^∥2≤23\lVert\hat{q}\rVert^{2}\leq\frac{2}{3}.

Proof.

By Lemma 4 the basis consists of antipodal pairs on three lines. All nonzero features lie on the lines by (10), so the covariance identity with three rank-one groups forces, as in (4), orthonormal directions with unit feature energy each. Let R1≥R2≥R3R_{1}\geq R_{2}\geq R_{3} be the line energies, ∑Rj≤1\sum R_{j}\leq 1. Select an antipodal canceling pair on the top-energy line and the best single point on each of the other two; per line the offset is 00 or at most RjR_{j}. Then ∥q^∥2≤R2+R3≤23\lVert\hat{q}\rVert^{2}\leq R_{2}+R_{3}\leq\frac{2}{3}, with 2+1+1=42+1+1=4 points. ∎

6.5 The main theorem for (3,4)(3,4)

Theorem 27.

Fw​(3,4)=53F_{\mathrm{w}}(3,4)=\frac{5}{3}.

Proof.

The lower bound is Theorem 13. For the upper bound, let DD be any dataset. If the features span a subspace of dimension ρ≤2\rho\leq 2, budget 4≥2​ρ4\geq 2\rho gives ratio 11 as in Theorem 9. If LD⋆=0L_{D}^{\star}=0, three independent features determine the realizable predictor. So assume full rank and LD⋆>0L_{D}^{\star}>0; whiten. If some point has ηi=0≠ξi\eta_{i}=0\neq\xi_{i}, Lemma 18 gives ratio at most 32+ε\frac{3}{2}+\varepsilon and we are done by the infimum; so assume (10). If the nonzero gradients spanned a proper subspace, some feature would lie outside it with zero gradient, contradicting (10) and full feature rank; so they span, and as in Theorem 8 they positively span ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}. Let BB be a minimum-cardinality positively spanning subset; |B|∈{4,5,6}|B|\in\{4,5,6\} by Lemma 4.

If |B|=4|B|=4: by Lemma 5(2), BB is a full-rank positive circuit; Lemma 2 recovers exactly with 44 points.

If |B|=5|B|=5: apply Theorem 20. If at any stage four gradients form a rank-33 positive circuit, Lemma 2 recovers exactly. Otherwise, in the coupled case Proposition 24 applies. In the split case, suppose some nonzero gradient gg lies outside V∪LV\cup L. Its minimal cone representation uses one triangle vertex aua_{u} and one pair gradient ℓ\ell, giving a cross relation g+α​au+β​ℓ=0g+\alpha a_{u}+\beta\ell=0 with α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0. The five gradients consisting of the triangle, gg and ℓ\ell then positively span ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}: the triangle positively spans VV, and the cross relation exhibits −ℓ-\ell as a positive combination. If some four of these five positively span, we get exact recovery; otherwise they form a five-vector positive basis containing two triangles that share aua_{u}, hence a coupled basis, and the previous case applies. If no such gradient exists, Proposition 25 applies.

If |B|=6|B|=6: for an extra gradient with components on all three lines, the rigidity construction of Lemma 6 with |S|=3|S|=3 produces a four-element positively spanning set, hence exact recovery. For an extra gradient on exactly two lines, the same construction produces a five-element positively spanning set, which reduces to the |B|≤5|B|\leq 5 cases. Otherwise all nonzero gradients lie on the three lines and Proposition 26 applies.

Every branch ends with a strictly convex objective of at most 44 points and ∥q^∥2≤23\lVert\hat{q}\rVert^{2}\leq\frac{2}{3}, or with the anchored branch at 32+ε\frac{3}{2}+\varepsilon. By (2) and the infimum in the definition, LD⋆​(4,A⋆)≤53​LD⋆L_{D}^{\star}(4;A^{\star})\leq\frac{5}{3}L_{D}^{\star}. ∎

Remark 30.

We do not know whether 32\frac{3}{2} is the exact supremum of LD⋆​(4,A⋆)/LD⋆L_{D}^{\star}(4;A^{\star})/L_{D}^{\star} over this class. We record this as a numerical observation only.

7 The budget 55 in dimension 44

This section proves Fw​(4,5)=2F_{\mathrm{w}}(4,5)=2. The lower bound is Theorem 13 at (d,k)=(4,1)(d,k)=(4,1). The upper bound combines four ingredients: interface versions of the results already proved, a completion lemma that finishes any low-rank positive circuit through quotient volume sampling, classifications of the minimal positive bases of ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4}, and a dimension-free extremal-basis argument that handles the one remaining configuration, the rectangle.

7.1 Interface lemmas

Theorem 31 (whitened (3,4)(3,4) interface).

Let {(ξi,ηi)}\{(\xi_{i},\eta_{i})\} be a whitened system in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} and ε>0\varepsilon>0. There are at most 44 indices and strictly positive weights whose objective is strictly convex with unique minimizer q^\hat{q} satisfying 1+∥q^∥2≤53+ε1+\lVert\hat{q}\rVert^{2}\leq\frac{5}{3}+\varepsilon.

Proof.

If the nonzero gradients span a proper subspace VV, some feature lies outside VV; its gradient lies in VV only if it vanishes, so this point has η0=0≠ξ0\eta_{0}=0\neq\xi_{0}, and Lemma 18 gives 32+ε\frac{3}{2}+\varepsilon. If they span ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} and some point has η0=0≠ξ0\eta_{0}=0\neq\xi_{0}, Lemma 18 applies again. Otherwise (10) holds, and the case analysis in the proof of Theorem 27 for spanning gradients runs verbatim inside the whitened system, producing finite strictly convex selections of at most 44 points with ∥q^∥2≤23\lVert\hat{q}\rVert^{2}\leq\frac{2}{3} in every branch. ∎

Corollary 32 (anchored reduction in ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4}).

Let a whitened system in ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4} contain a point with η0=0\eta_{0}=0 and ξ0≠0\xi_{0}\neq 0. Then for every ε>0\varepsilon>0 there is a strictly convex, strictly positively weighted selection of at most 55 points with 1+∥q^∥2≤53+ε1+\lVert\hat{q}\rVert^{2}\leq\frac{5}{3}+\varepsilon.

Proof.

Project to W=ξ0⟂≅ℝ3W=\xi_{0}^{\perp}\cong\mathbb{R}^{3}; the projected family is a whitened system on WW, as in Lemma 18. Fix δm↓0\delta_{m}\downarrow 0. By Theorem 31 there is a finite objective GmG_{m} of at most 44 original points whose restriction to WW is strictly convex with minimizer umu_{m} and 1+∥um∥2≤53+δm1+\lVert u_{m}\rVert^{2}\leq\frac{5}{3}+\delta_{m}; if the construction of GmG_{m} itself involves an inner anchor penalty, fix that inner parameter first at a finite value achieving the bound. Then add the outer penalty λ​⟨q,ξ0⟩2\lambda\langle q,\xi_{0}\rangle^{2} and apply Lemma 17: for a large finite λm\lambda_{m} the unique minimizer qmq_{m} of the five-point objective satisfies |∥qm∥2−∥um∥2|≤δm\bigl|\lVert q_{m}\rVert^{2}-\lVert u_{m}\rVert^{2}\bigr|\leq\delta_{m}. Let m→∞m\to\infty. ∎

Lemma 33 (minimal cone representation).

Let BB positively span ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m} and g≠0g\neq 0. Then −g=∑t∈Tαt​t-g=\sum_{t\in T}\alpha_{t}t for some linearly independent T⊆BT\subseteq B and αt>0\alpha_{t}>0, and T∪{g}T\cup\{g\} is a positive circuit of rank |T||T|.

The strictly positive relation g+∑αt​t=0g+\sum\alpha_{t}t=0 on an independent support is a positive circuit. ∎

Lemma 35 (circuit-star).

Let a whitened system in ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4} contain a rank-22 positive triangle circuit of gradients with plane PP, and suppose every projected feature ΠP⟂​ξi\Pi_{P^{\perp}}\xi_{i} lies on one of two lines of P⟂P^{\perp}. 7.3 Branch reductions

Throughout this subsection the system is a whitened system in ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4} satisfying

gi=0⟹ξi=0,g_{i}=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \xi_{i}=0, (13)

Proposition 36.

If |B|=5|B|=5, exact recovery with 55 points.

Proof.

Lemma 5(2): BB is a rank-44 positive circuit; Lemma 2. ∎

Proposition 37 (size-66 classification).

Let |B|=6|B|=6. Then either some four gradients of BB form a positive circuit of rank 33, in which case Lemma 34 gives ∥q^∥2≤E⁡(P)≤1\lVert\hat{q}\rVert^{2}\leq E(P)\leq 1 with 55 points, or BB is the disjoint union of two rank-22 triangle circuits spanning complementary planes.

Proof.

Let KK be the kernel of the matrix with columns BB; dimK=2\dim K=2, and 𝒞=K∩ℝ+6\mathcal{C}=K\cap\mathbb{R}^{6}_{+} is a two-dimensional pointed cone with a strictly positive interior point, hence two extreme rays with circuit supports S,TS,T covering [6][6] (Lemma 5). A support of size 55 would be a rank-44 circuit, positively spanning with five elements against minimality; size 11 is impossible; equal supports would give a two-dimensional dependence space on a circuit. So |S|,|T|∈{2,3,4}|S|,|T|\in\{2,3,4\} with |S∪T|=6|S\cup T|=6, leaving (3,3)(3,3) disjoint, (4,3)(4,3) sharing one, (4,4)(4,4) sharing two, and (4,2)(4,2) disjoint. In the last three cases the size-44 support is a positive circuit of rank 33. The case (3,3)(3,3) disjoint gives two triangles whose planes are complementary because BB has rank 44. ∎

Proposition 38 (two blocks without cross gradients).

Let B=A∪CB=A\cup C be two disjoint triangles with complementary planes U,VU,V, and suppose all nonzero gradients lie in U∪VU\cup V. Then a five-point strictly convex selection achieves ∥q^∥2≤1\lVert\hat{q}\rVert^{2}\leq 1.

Then I=HU+HVI=H_{U}+H_{V} with rank⁡HU=rank⁡HV=2\operatorname{rank}H_{U}=\operatorname{rank}H_{V}=2; since 0⪯HU,HV⪯I0\preceq H_{U},H_{V}\preceq I and the ranks are complementary, U⟂VU\perp V and HU=PUH_{U}=P_{U}, HV=PVH_{V}=P_{V}. Definition 39.

In the two-block case, a cross gradient of type (i,j)(i,j) is a nonzero gradient hh with minimal cone representation h+α​ai+β​cj=0h+\alpha a_{i}+\beta c_{j}=0, α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0, where ai∈Aa_{i}\in A and cj∈Cc_{j}\in C. Proposition 40 (shared-endpoint crosses).

In the two-block case, suppose cross gradients occur and all cross types share an endpoint, that is, all use the same aia_{i} or all use the same cjc_{j}. Suppose also that no four gradients form a rank-33 positive circuit and no five gradients positively span. Then a five-point strictly convex selection achieves ∥q^∥2≤1\lVert\hat{q}\rVert^{2}\leq 1.

Proof.

First reduce the extra gradients. By Lemma 33 each nonzero gradient outside BB has a minimal cone support in BB of size at most 44. Size 44 gives a rank-44 five-point positive circuit, which positively spans and is excluded; size 33 gives a rank-33 circuit, excluded. Supports of size 11 or 22 inside one triangle stay in that triangle’s plane, and the mixed supports are exactly the cross gradients. Say all cross types use a1a_{1}. Fix one cross circuit {h,a1,cj}\{h,a_{1},c_{j}\} and let P=span⁡(a1,cj)P=\operatorname{span}(a_{1},c_{j}), a plane carrying this positive triangle circuit. Project to P⟂P^{\perp}. The AA-plane maps to the line spanned by the image of a2a_{2}; the CC-plane maps to the line spanned by the images of the cj′c_{j^{\prime}}, j′≠jj^{\prime}\neq j, which is one line since CC’s plane is two-dimensional and cjc_{j} maps to zero. A cross gradient of type (1,j′)(1,j^{\prime}) maps into the CC-line since h′=−α​a1−β​cj′h^{\prime}=-\alpha a_{1}-\beta c_{j^{\prime}} and a1a_{1} maps to zero. Gradients in PP map to zero. So all projected features lie on two lines and Lemma 35 applies. ∎

Proposition 41 (size 77).

If |B|=7|B|=7, a five-point strictly convex selection achieves ∥q^∥2≤1\lVert\hat{q}\rVert^{2}\leq 1.

Proof.

If some four gradients of BB form a rank-33 positive circuit, Lemma 34 finishes. Otherwise all extreme-ray circuits of the dependence cone of BB have size at most 33. They cannot all be antipodal pairs: disjoint pairs cannot cover seven coordinates, and two pairs sharing a vector force two elements on one ray, one of them removable. So there is a triangle circuit C0={p,q,u}C_{0}=\{p,q,u\} with plane V=pos⁡(C0)V=\operatorname{pos}(C_{0}).

By Lemma 7 the projections of the other four vectors to ℝ4/V\mathbb{R}^{4}/V form a positive basis of the two-dimensional quotient of size 44, which by Lemma 4 consists of two antipodal projected pairs:

v+λr=p1∈V,w+μs=p2∈V,λ,μ>0.v+\lambda r=p_{1}\in V,\qquad w+\mu s=p_{2}\in V,\qquad\lambda,\mu>0.

Represent −p1-p_{1} over the triangle C0C_{0} minimally. A support of two triangle vectors would give a rank-33 four-point circuit, excluded; so p1=0p_{1}=0 or p1p_{1} is a negative multiple of a single triangle vector, and likewise p2p_{2}. If the two nonzero shifts anchored at different triangle vectors ca≠cbc_{a}\neq c_{b}, then −ca∈pos⁡{r,v}-c_{a}\in\operatorname{pos}\{r,v\} and −cb∈pos⁡{s,w}-c_{b}\in\operatorname{pos}\{s,w\}, and the triangle relation would put the third vector ccc_{c} in pos⁡{r,v,s,w}\operatorname{pos}\{r,v,s,w\}, making it removable; contradiction. So after renaming the shared anchor qq,

q+p+u=0,v+λr+τq=0,w+μs+σq=0,τ,σ≥0.q+p+u=0,\qquad v+\lambda r+\tau q=0,\qquad w+\mu s+\sigma q=0,\qquad\tau,\sigma\geq 0.

Suppose τ,σ>0\tau,\sigma>0 and set P0=span⁡(p,q)P_{0}=\operatorname{span}(p,q), P1=span⁡(q,r)P_{1}=\operatorname{span}(q,r), P2=span⁡(q,s)P_{2}=\operatorname{span}(q,s). All seven basis vectors lie in P0∪P1∪P2P_{0}\cup P_{1}\cup P_{2}. Consider any extra nonzero gradient. Its minimal cone support has size at most 22: size 44 gives a rank-44 five-point circuit and exact recovery, size 33 a rank-33 circuit and completion. Supports of size 11, and two-element supports drawn from one leaf group or from a leaf group together with qq, lie inside one of the three planes. If a two-element support takes its vectors from two different leaf groups among {p,u},{r,v},{s,w}\{p,u\},\{r,v\},\{s,w\}, the gradient forms a positive triangle with them, and the unused third group together with qq forms another positive triangle; the two planes are complementary, so six of the gradients positively span ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4}, contradicting |B|=7|B|=7 as minimum cardinality. Hence every extra gradient lies in P0∪P1∪P2P_{0}\cup P_{1}\cup P_{2}. Project to P0⟂P_{0}^{\perp}: the planes P1,P2P_{1},P_{2} become two lines, and Lemma 35 with the central triangle finishes.

If τ=σ=0\tau=\sigma=0, the leaves are detached antipodal pairs. A two-element support mixing the two pairs forms with the central triangle two triangles in complementary planes, hence a six-point positively spanning set, contradiction. Every other support is contained in {p,q,u}∪{r,v}\{p,q,u\}\cup\{r,v\} or in {p,q,u}∪{s,w}\{p,q,u\}\cup\{s,w\}. The resulting gradient need not itself lie in P0P_{0} or on a pair line; but under the projection along P0P_{0} its central component vanishes, so its image lies on the projected line of the pair it uses. Hence the projected features occupy two lines and Lemma 35 applies.

If exactly one shift vanishes, say σ=0\sigma=0 and τ>0\tau>0, the excluded mixed supports are as follows; in each case the exhibited triangle pairs with a complementary triangle present in the configuration to give a six-point positively spanning set. A support mixing {s,w}\{s,w\} with {r,v}\{r,v\} pairs with the central triangle {q,p,u}\{q,p,u\}. A support mixing {p,u}\{p,u\} with {s,w}\{s,w\} pairs with the leaf triangle {q,r,v}\{q,r,v\}. If a cross with support mixing {p,u}\{p,u\} and {r,v}\{r,v\} exists, fix one such cross triangle {g0,x,z}\{g_{0},x,z\} and take P=span⁡(x,z)P=\operatorname{span}(x,z) as anchor plane; then a support {q,s}\{q,s\} or {q,w}\{q,w\} pairs with this cross triangle and is excluded as well. Modulo PP, both nondegenerate triangles project to the line of π⁡(q)\pi(q), further crosses of the same mixed type project into the same line, and the detached pair projects to a second line; Lemma 35 applies. If no such cross exists, every remaining support is contained in {p,q,u,r,v}\{p,q,u,r,v\} or in {p,q,u}∪{s,w}\{p,q,u\}\cup\{s,w\} or in {q,s,w}\{q,s,w\}; in each case the projection along P0P_{0} kills the central component, and the image lies on the projected rr-line or the projected ss-line. Two lines again, and Lemma 35 applies. ∎

Proposition 42 (size 88).

If |B|=8|B|=8, a five-point strictly convex selection achieves ∥q^∥2≤34\lVert\hat{q}\rVert^{2}\leq\frac{3}{4}.

Proof.

Minimum cardinality 88 means no seven nonzero gradients positively span, so Lemma 6 puts all nonzero gradients on four lines, and by (13) all nonzero features as well. The covariance identity with four rank-one groups forces orthonormal directions and unit energy per line as in (4). Select a canceling antipodal pair on the line of largest residual energy and the best single point on each other line; the offsets are 00 and at most RjR_{j}. The three smaller energies sum to at most 34\frac{3}{4}. ∎

7.4 The rectangle branch

We now treat the rectangle branch of Definition 39. Relabel so that the two given cross types are attached to the rays of a1,a2∈Aa_{1},a_{2}\in A and c1,c2∈Cc_{1},c_{2}\in C, with A={a0,a1,a2}A=\{a_{0},a_{1},a_{2}\}, C={c0,c1,c2}C=\{c_{0},c_{1},c_{2}\}, normalized by

a0+a1+a2=0,c0+c1+c2=0,a_{0}+a_{1}+a_{2}=0,\qquad c_{0}+c_{1}+c_{2}=0,

Lemma 43 (off-side points).

In the rectangle branch, assume no four gradients form a rank-33 positive circuit and no five gradients form a rank-44 positive circuit. Then every nonzero gradient not on a side line is strictly 44-generated.

Proof.

First the basis vectors and cross points. Substituting the triangle relations into the cross relations,

a0=1p​h+1r​k+qp​c1+sr​c2,c0=1q​h+1s​k+pq​a1+rs​a2,a_{0}=\tfrac{1}{p}\,h+\tfrac{1}{r}\,k+\tfrac{q}{p}\,c_{1}+\tfrac{s}{r}\,c_{2},\qquad c_{0}=\tfrac{1}{q}\,h+\tfrac{1}{s}\,k+\tfrac{p}{q}\,a_{1}+\tfrac{r}{s}\,a_{2},

and the generators are independent: in the basis (a1,a2,c1,c2)(a_{1},a_{2},c_{1},c_{2}) the matrix of (h,k,c1,c2)(h,k,c_{1},c_{2}) has determinant p​r≠0pr\neq 0, and symmetrically for c0c_{0}. More generally, any cross gradient gg with g+x​ai+y​cj=0g+x\,a_{i}+y\,c_{j}=0, x,y>0x,y>0, satisfies

Next the in-plane points; we write the AA-plane case, the CC-plane being symmetric. Let gg be a nonzero gradient in the AA-plane and off the side lines, and take its minimal cone support over BB (Lemma 33), of size at most 44. Size 44 would give a rank-44 five-point positive circuit and size 33 a rank-33 circuit, both excluded by hypothesis, so the support has at most two elements. It cannot involve an element of CC: the planes are complementary, so if −g=α​ai+β​cj-g=\alpha a_{i}+\beta c_{j} with β>0\beta>0, then β​cj=−g−α​ai\beta c_{j}=-g-\alpha a_{i} lies in the AA-plane, forcing cj=0c_{j}=0; a support inside CC alone would put gg in both planes, hence g=0g=0. The case g=−x​a0−y​a2g=-x\,a_{0}-y\,a_{2} is symmetric, with L1L_{1} as the ray boundary. Hence in the remaining configuration every off-side nonzero gradient is strictly 44-generated. ∎

The excluded cases in Lemma 43 are not losses: a rank-33 circuit yields ∥q^∥2≤1\lVert\hat{q}\rVert^{2}\leq 1 by Lemma 34, and a rank-44 five-point circuit yields exact recovery by Lemma 2. It remains to handle the configuration in which every off-side point is strictly 44-generated.

We pass to projective coordinates. Proposition 46 (rectangle closure).

In the rectangle branch, under (13), either some selection of at most 55 points achieves ∥q^∥2≤1\lVert\hat{q}\rVert^{2}\leq 1 outright, or the extremal basis hypothesis holds and the infimum over five-point selections of the excess is at most 11.

Proof.

If some four gradients form a rank-33 positive circuit or some five form a rank-44 circuit, Lemma 34 or Lemma 2 finishes. Otherwise Lemma 43 applies: every off-side nonzero point is strictly 44-generated. On each side line LlL_{l} fix a reference direction and pick the data point plp_{l} on LlL_{l} of maximal |θ||\theta|, where v=θ⋅(reference)v=\theta\cdot(\text{reference}); the four side lines carry the basis rays a1,a2,c1,c2a_{1},a_{2},c_{1},c_{2}, so each holds at least one point, and the four chosen points are independent since a1,a2a_{1},a_{2} span the AA-plane and c1,c2c_{1},c_{2} the complementary CC-plane. So every point with |z|>1|z|>1 is off-side, hence strictly 44-generated, and Lemma 45 with d=4d=4 applies. ∎

Theorem 47.

Fw​(4,5)=2F_{\mathrm{w}}(4,5)=2.

Proof.

The lower bound is Theorem 13. For the upper bound, let DD be arbitrary. If the feature rank is ρ≤2\rho\leq 2, budget 5≥2​ρ5\geq 2\rho gives ratio 11; if ρ=3\rho=3, the problem is isometric to dimension 33 with budget 5=2⋅3−15=2\cdot 3-1, and Theorem 9 gives 43<2\frac{4}{3}<2. If LD⋆=0L_{D}^{\star}=0, four independent features finish. Otherwise whiten. If some point has ηi=0≠ξi\eta_{i}=0\neq\xi_{i}, Corollary 32 gives 53+ε<2\frac{5}{3}+\varepsilon<2. So assume (13); as before the nonzero gradients span, hence positively span, ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4}. Take a minimum-cardinality positively spanning subset BB.

|B|=5|B|=5: Proposition 36, excess 00. |B|=6|B|=6: Proposition 37 either finishes with excess at most 11 or leaves two complementary triangles B=A∪CB=A\cup C with planes U,VU,V. In the latter case, first reduce the gradients outside BB by their minimal cone supports over BB (Lemma 33): a support of size 44 gives a rank-44 five-point positive circuit and exact recovery by Lemma 2; a support of size 33 gives a rank-33 circuit and Lemma 34 finishes with excess at most 11. If neither occurs, every extra gradient has support of size at most 22; supports of size 11, or of size 22 inside one triangle, lie in U∪VU\cup V, and the mixed two-element supports are exactly the cross gradients of Definition 39. Now the trichotomy is exhaustive: with no cross gradients, all nonzero gradients lie in U∪VU\cup V and Proposition 38 applies; with cross gradients all sharing an endpoint, note first that if any four gradients form a rank-33 positive circuit then Lemma 34 finishes, and that no five gradients positively span since BB has minimum cardinality 66, so Proposition 40 applies; with two non-sharing cross types, Proposition 46. |B|=7|B|=7: Proposition 41. |B|=8|B|=8: Proposition 42.

Every branch gives excess at most 11, either by a finite strictly convex selection or as an infimum, so LD⋆​(5,A⋆)≤2​LD⋆L_{D}^{\star}(5;A^{\star})\leq 2L_{D}^{\star}. ∎

8 Three obstructions

The proof of Theorem 47 runs through sign-cone geometry rather than through any of three shorter routes that one might try first. This section shows that each of those routes fails, by explicit counterexamples. Every numerical claim in this section is a finite exact rational computation; the derivations appear in the proofs, and scripts re-verifying each claimed fraction in exact arithmetic are available from the author.

8.1 Low-dimensional circuit covers fail

Lemma 33 controls every extra gradient by a low-rank positive circuit. It is tempting to hope that these circuit flats can be chosen with small total dimension, so that a partition-style argument as in Section 5 finishes. This fails already at the minimal cell.

Proposition 48 (rectangle obstruction).

In ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4} let

a1=e1,a2=e2,a3=−e1−e2,b1=e3,b2=e4,b3=−e3−e4,\displaystyle a_{1}=e_{1},\quad a_{2}=e_{2},\quad a_{3}=-e_{1}-e_{2},\qquad b_{1}=e_{3},\quad b_{2}=e_{4},\quad b_{3}=-e_{3}-e_{4},
h1=−e1−e3,h2=−e2−e4,\displaystyle h_{1}=-e_{1}-e_{3},\qquad h_{2}=-e_{2}-e_{4},

and G={a1,a2,a3,b1,b2,b3,h1,h2}G=\{a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},b_{1},b_{2},b_{3},h_{1},h_{2}\}. Then GG positively spans ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4}; no subset of at most five vectors positively spans; the positive circuits of GG are exactly {a1,a2,a3}\{a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}\}, {b1,b2,b3}\{b_{1},b_{2},b_{3}\}, {a1,b1,h1}\{a_{1},b_{1},h_{1}\}, {a2,b2,h2}\{a_{2},b_{2},h_{2}\}; and any cover of GG by circuit flats needs four planes, of total dimension 88.

Proof.

A nonnegative dependence ∑λi​ai+∑μi​bi+ν1​h1+ν2​h2=0\sum\lambda_{i}a_{i}+\sum\mu_{i}b_{i}+\nu_{1}h_{1}+\nu_{2}h_{2}=0 forces, coordinate by coordinate, λ1=λ3+ν1\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{3}+\nu_{1}, λ2=λ3+ν2\lambda_{2}=\lambda_{3}+\nu_{2}, μ1=μ3+ν1\mu_{1}=\mu_{3}+\nu_{1}, μ2=μ3+ν2\mu_{2}=\mu_{3}+\nu_{2}. The dependence cone is therefore generated by four extreme rays, obtained by setting one of λ3,μ3,ν1,ν2\lambda_{3},\mu_{3},\nu_{1},\nu_{2} to one and the others to zero; these are the four listed triangles, and there are no other positive circuits. A positively spanning subset must support a strictly positive dependence whose support spans ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4}; single circuits have rank 22, two circuits sharing a direction span at most rank 33, and the two complementary unions {a1,a2,a3,b1,b2,b3}\{a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},b_{1},b_{2},b_{3}\} and {a1,b1,h1,a2,b2,h2}\{a_{1},b_{1},h_{1},a_{2},b_{2},h_{2}\} have six elements each. Finally a3,b3,h1,h2a_{3},b_{3},h_{1},h_{2} each belong to exactly one circuit plane, so all four planes are needed. ∎

The associated regression instance is harmless for the risk question: with features 2​e1,2​e2,−e1−e2,2​e3,2​e4,−e3−e4,−e1−e3,−e2−e42e_{1},2e_{2},-e_{1}-e_{2},2e_{3},2e_{4},-e_{3}-e_{4},-e_{1}-e_{3},-e_{2}-e_{4} and all labels 11, the rows sum to zero, w⋆=0w^{\star}=0, LD⋆=1L_{D}^{\star}=1, and the five-point selection of the first five rows with weights (316,316,12,116,116)(\frac{3}{16},\frac{3}{16},\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{16},\frac{1}{16}) outputs (−114,−114,12,12)(-\frac{1}{14},-\frac{1}{14},\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}) with full risk 107<2\frac{10}{7}<2. The obstruction concerns proof technique, not the value of Fw​(4,5)F_{\mathrm{w}}(4,5).

The failure mode is instructive. The counterexample lives in a near-degenerate boundary layer: the cross directions are smaller than the block directions by a factor of 100100, yet carry constant residual mass. Standard log-random parameter sweeps miss this layer; ours did, over hundreds of thousands of samples, before the construction above was found by analyzing the boundary. 9 Constructive selection algorithms

All upper bounds in this paper are constructive in the following sense. Working in exact real arithmetic over the input, and given ε>0\varepsilon>0, each procedure below outputs a selection whose risk ratio is at most the stated bound plus ε\varepsilon, using a number of arithmetic operations polynomial in NN for the fixed dimensions concerned. The ε\varepsilon enters only through the branches that use penalty limits or sign-cone closures, where a finite penalty parameter or a finite interior point must be chosen as a function of ε\varepsilon; all other branches output selections attaining their bounds exactly. We record the procedures; none has been optimized for running time.

Budget 2​d−12d-1.

Given DD: compute the feature span and LD⋆L_{D}^{\star}; in the rank-deficient or realizable cases return the corresponding exact certificates. Otherwise whiten and form the gradients. If the nonzero gradients span a proper subspace, return the Steinitz certificate plus rank-completing zero-gradient points. Otherwise repeatedly delete gradients while the remainder still positively spans, testing positive spanning by one linear program per deletion; the terminal set is a positive basis of size at most 2​d2d. If its size is at most 2​d−12d-1, solve for the strictly positive dependence and return it. If its size is 2​d2d, scan the remaining gradients: any gradient off the two-per-line structure yields, by the construction inside Lemma 6, a positively spanning set of at most 2​d−12d-1 gradients, and we return its certificate. Next check for a point with ηi=0≠ξi\eta_{i}=0\neq\xi_{i}: if one exists, return the certificate of the zero-gradient branch of Theorem 8, a canceling pair on each of d−1d-1 lines plus this point. Only then do all features lie on the dd lines; compute the per-line residual energies, select the best single point on the lightest line and canceling pairs elsewhere.

Budget 44, dimension 33.

After the same preprocessing: if an anchor point (ηi=0≠ξi\eta_{i}=0\neq\xi_{i}) exists, run the d=2d=2 procedure on the orthogonal complement and penalize the anchor with a large finite weight. Otherwise extract a minimum-cardinality positively spanning set. Size 44: return the circuit. Size 55: identify the two extremal circuits of the dependence cone; in the coupled case, classify the extra gradients by their minimal cone supports, detect a four-point rank-33 circuit if present, otherwise compute the at most three circuit-plane energies, take the plane maximizing R⁡(P)R(P), and pair its triangle with the point minimizing ηj2/⟨u,ξj⟩2\eta_{j}^{2}/\langle u,\xi_{j}\rangle^{2} off the plane; in the split case, first test every nonzero gradient for membership in V∪LV\cup L: a gradient outside triggers the reduction of Theorem 27 to an exact four-point certificate or to the coupled case; only when all gradients lie in V∪LV\cup L compare RLR_{L} against 2​RV2R_{V} and return the better of the two selections of Proposition 25. Size 66: handle cross-line gradients as in Theorem 27, otherwise select a canceling pair on the heaviest line and best single points elsewhere.

Budget 55, dimension 44.

The branch structure of Theorem 47 is algorithmic in the same way. The new ingredients are the following. A minimum-cardinality positively spanning subset is found by enumerating gradient subsets of size at most 2​d2d in increasing size and testing positive spanning by one linear program each; for fixed dimension this is polynomially many checks in NN. A support-minimal cone representation is obtained from any feasible nonnegative representation by repeatedly deleting an element whose removal keeps feasibility, or, for fixed dimension, by enumerating candidate supports of size at most 44 directly; an arbitrary feasible solution of the linear program need not have minimal support, and the branch selection depends on the support size. In the two-triangle case every extra gradient is first classified by its support size, returning the five-point exact certificate at size 44 and the completion selection at size 33 before any cross analysis. The size-66 and size-77 bases are classified through the extreme rays of their dependence cones. In the rectangle branch, the extremal basis is computed by fixing a reference direction on each side line, writing each point on the line as v=θ⋅(reference)v=\theta\cdot(\text{reference}), taking the point of maximal absolute scalar |θ||\theta| on each of the four side lines, and solving one 4×44\times 4 linear system for qBq_{B}. If ∥qB∥≤1\lVert q_{B}\rVert\leq 1, return the four-point interpolation. Otherwise anchor at the maximal evaluation |zi||z_{i}| and read off its strict generation vi=∑jκj​wjv_{i}=\sum_{j}\kappa_{j}w_{j}; if K=∑jκj=1K=\sum_{j}\kappa_{j}=1, return the five-point interpolation at q∗q_{\ast}; if K>1K>1, pick the interior point qcq_{c} with side values c∈(1/K,1)c\in(1/K,1), choose t>0t>0 small enough that the risk of (1−t)​q∗+t​qc(1-t)q_{\ast}+t\,q_{c} is within the prescribed ε\varepsilon, and return the sign-cone weights of Lemma 44 at that point.

Block systems.

For orthogonal circuit-block systems with known blocks, the optimal budget allocation of Theorem 15 is computed by sorting the products rj​Rjr_{j}R_{j} and completing the kk largest blocks.

10 Discussion and open problems

The conjecture.

All exact values proved here, together with the block-model minimax value of Section 5, support the following.

Conjecture 10.54.

Fw​(d,d+k)=1+Γd,kF_{\mathrm{w}}(d,d+k)=1+\Gamma_{d,k} for all 1≤k≤d−11\leq k\leq d-1.

The conjecture holds at k=d−1k=d-1 (Corollary 11), at (d,k)=(3,1)(d,k)=(3,1) (Theorem 27) and at (d,k)=(4,1)(d,k)=(4,1) (Theorem 47); and its value is the exact minimax answer on the class of orthogonal circuit-block systems (Corollary 16). As auxiliary evidence, the randomized stress tests in dimensions two and three, and exhaustive support enumeration with numerical and randomized weight search on the structured instances in dimensions four and five, with seeded scripts available from the author, produced no instance exceeding 1+Γd,k1+\Gamma_{d,k}; further exploratory searches in higher dimensions, not packaged reproducibly, found none either. Per-weight solves are exact, but the weight search is not a global optimization, and we cite all of this as diagnostics, not as verification. The smallest open cell is (d,n)=(4,6)(d,n)=(4,6), with conjectured value 32\frac{3}{2}.

What remains for a general upper bound.

The proofs of Theorems 27 and 47 share a shape. Away from degenerate branches, the nonzero gradients contain a minimal positive basis; the basis decomposes into circuits; and the losses are covered by circuit flats plus a controlled set of coupling gradients. When the couplings are absent, the system is an orthogonal block system, and Theorem 15 is exact. When couplings are present, they open cheaper selections; in every case analyzed here, coupling helps the selector, and the worst case degenerates back to the orthogonal block extremals. The extremal-basis lemma (Lemma 45) is dimension-free. As a heuristic, its hypothesis is obstructed on simplex-block extremals with a block of dimension at least two: calibrating a basis inside the blocks leaves a missed vertex with evaluation of magnitude equal to its block dimension, and no cross ears exist to generate it. On all-one-dimensional blocks the hypothesis can hold vacuously, and the lemma then gives the harmless bound of excess 11. Making this interplay precise is part of the program below. Turning this dichotomy into a theorem, a statement that every gradient system is dominated by a circuit-block system that is no better for the selector, is in our view the central remaining step; it would prove Conjecture 10.54 in full.

Further questions.

Three natural directions. First, the unweighted and vector-valued variants of the problem (Questions 3 and 4 of Hanneke et al., 2025b) interact with the present geometry through the same gradient structure, and it would be interesting to see which parts transfer. Second, our selections are constructive but not optimized; the complexity of computing an optimal weighted selection for a given dataset is open. Third, the classifications of small positive bases developed here, in particular the size-77 common-anchor form in ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4}, may be of independent use in derivative-free optimization, where positive spanning sets are a basic primitive.
